description: Steve Biko, SASO and the Durban strikes — new fronts opening in the resistance.
content_html:
A New Philosophy of Liberation

After the Rivonia convictions and the “long silence” of the mid-1960s, resistance inside South Africa looked fragmented. It was in this context that a new philosophy emerged: Black Consciousness. Its central idea was that apartheid’s deepest damage was psychological — it had made black South Africans internalise a sense of inferiority. Before political liberation could happen, mental liberation must come first.

Steve Biko was the movement’s defining intellectual. Born in 1946 in King William’s Town, he became politically active while studying medicine at the University of Natal. He was a brilliant writer and speaker who argued, in plain language, that black people had to reject the white liberal view that integration with white society was the goal, and instead build pride, solidarity and culture on their own terms.

Key Fact

The South African Students’ Organisation (SASO) was founded in 1969, separating black students from white-liberal-dominated student organisations. Its founding argument was that black students must organise independently to build consciousness and self-reliance.

SASO and the Black People’s Convention

SASO spread rapidly through the black universities created by the Bantu Education system — in an irony of history, the very institutions designed to restrict black education became hotbeds of political organising. In 1972, the Black People’s Convention (BPC) was founded to carry Black Consciousness beyond the campuses into community organisations, sports clubs and cultural groups.

Mamphela Ramphele was among the key figures in the BCM. Women’s groups linked to the BCM organised welfare, health clinics and community centres in townships, showing that Black Consciousness was as much about building community capacity as about political protest.

Between January and March 1973, a wave of strikes swept through Durban involving approximately 100,000 workers in docks, factories, transport and municipal services. The Durban strikes were significant for several reasons. First, they demonstrated that black workers could organise collectively despite the apartheid government’s ban on black trade union membership. Second, they forced employers and the government to acknowledge that low wages and the pass system were economically as well as politically unsustainable.

The Durban strikes were largely peaceful. Workers walked out, demanded higher wages and, in many cases, secured modest increases. They were not led by a single organisation and were largely spontaneous — which made them harder for the government to suppress than a formal strike by a named union. They accelerated trade union organising: by the mid-1970s, embryonic independent black trade unions were emerging, which would become the basis for the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU) founded in 1985.

Steve Biko’s Death in Custody

Steve Biko was banned (restricted from speaking publicly or meeting more than one person at a time) by the security police from 1973. On 18 August 1977, he was arrested at a police roadblock near Grahamstown. During interrogation at Port Elizabeth security police headquarters, he sustained severe brain injuries. He was transported 1,200 kilometres to Pretoria, naked and unconscious, in the back of a Land Rover. He died in a Pretoria prison on 12 September 1977.

An inquest court initially found no one criminally responsible for his death; the inquest was reopened in 1997 and found that members of the security police had caused his fatal injuries. The apartheid government at the time claimed he had died from a hunger strike, a claim that was false and was exposed by the inquest evidence. Biko’s death provoked international outrage. In October 1977, the government banned all the main BCM organisations.

Key Fact

Steve Biko died in police custody on 12 September 1977, from brain injuries sustained during interrogation. The government banned all major Black Consciousness organisations the following month. Biko’s death became one of the most powerful symbols of apartheid brutality.

Black Consciousness filled the organisational vacuum left by the Rivonia imprisonments. It helped shape the generation of students who would lead the Soweto uprising of 1976. Its emphasis on cultural pride and psychological liberation influenced how South Africans of all generations understood their struggle. However, the BCM did not form a conventional political party and its relationship with the ANC in exile was sometimes tense — the ANC’s multiracial philosophy differed from the BCM’s emphasis on black self-organisation.
exam_tip_html: Black Consciousness questions often ask you to “explain why” it developed or “explain the impact” of BCM. Be precise: the key impact inside South Africa was psychological (rebuilding pride after Rivonia), organisational (filling the vacuum left by the ANC’s banning) and generational (shaping the students of 1976). Biko’s death is also a key event with consequences — don’t just describe it; explain what changed because of it (banning of BCM organisations, international pressure).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Black Consciousness, developed through SASO from 1969, argued that psychological liberation must precede political liberation, filling the organisational vacuum left by the Rivonia imprisonments.
  • The Durban strike wave of 1973 showed the potential of black worker organisation and accelerated the growth of independent trade unions that would play a major role in the 1980s resistance.
  • Steve Biko’s death in police custody on 12 September 1977 confirmed for the world the brutal reality of apartheid state violence; the banning of BCM organisations that followed failed to suppress the movement’s influence.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Black Consciousness Movement in South Africa.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names BCM AND gives a precise feature, e.g. it argued that psychological liberation — rejecting internalised inferiority — must precede political liberation; or SASO was founded in 1969 by Steve Biko to organise black students independently. Secure: Correct identification with some supporting detail. Developing: Vague reference to black pride or student movement. Emerging: Minimal or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Durban strike wave of 1973.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per feature. Mastering: Two precise features — e.g. (1) approximately 100,000 workers in docks, factories, transport and municipal services participated; (2) strikes were largely peaceful and spontaneous, making them harder to suppress. Secure: Two features identified, one with clear detail. Developing: Two features with limited detail. Emerging: One feature or very general response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Black Consciousness Movement emerged in South Africa in the late 1960s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more fully developed reasons — e.g. (1) the Rivonia imprisonments had created an organisational vacuum inside South Africa; (2) the ANC and PAC were banned, leaving a political space for a new approach; (3) Bantu Education had concentrated politically active students in black universities. Each with specific evidence. Secure: Two reasons with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-developed reason or two underdeveloped points. Emerging: Descriptive account.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of trade unions in the early 1970s challenged the apartheid system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two fully developed points — e.g. (1) the Durban strikes demonstrated that black workers could organise collectively despite the legal ban on black trade unions; (2) they forced employers and government to recognise that the pass system and low wages were economically unsustainable. Secure: Two points with good supporting detail. Developing: One well-explained point. Emerging: Vague or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Outline the significance of Steve Biko's death in police custody in September 1977.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Key facts (death 12 September 1977, brain injuries from interrogation, government's false hunger-strike claim) AND significance: international outrage, banning of BCM organisations, symbol of apartheid brutality. Secure: Correct account with two points of significance. Developing: Basic account with limited significance analysis. Emerging: Very general response.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Black Consciousness Movement in keeping resistance to apartheid alive during the 1970s? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument assessing BCM's significance (filled organisational vacuum, shaped Soweto generation, international impact of Biko's death) against other factors (ANC in exile under Tambo, Durban strike-driven trade unionism, continuing ANC underground); reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides. Developing: Descriptive coverage of BCM with limited comparison to other factors. Emerging: Narrative description.

The Black People's Convention (BPC), founded in 1972, was created to spread Black Consciousness ideas _____ university campuses.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the core argument of Black Consciousness?
flashcard_questions.a: Psychological liberation — rejecting internalised inferiority — must precede political liberation

flashcard_questions.q: When was SASO founded and by whom?
flashcard_questions.a: 1969, by Steve Biko — to organise black students independently of white liberal organisations

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Black People's Convention (BPC)?
flashcard_questions.a: A broader political umbrella body founded 1972 to spread Black Consciousness beyond universities

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Durban strike wave?
flashcard_questions.a: January to March 1973 — approximately 100,000 workers involved

flashcard_questions.q: What made the Durban strikes hard for the government to suppress?
flashcard_questions.a: They were largely spontaneous and not led by a single named organisation

flashcard_questions.q: When did Steve Biko die and how?
flashcard_questions.a: 12 September 1977 — brain injuries sustained during interrogation in police custody

flashcard_questions.q: What did the apartheid government falsely claim about Biko's death?
flashcard_questions.a: That he had died from a hunger strike — contradicted by inquest evidence

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to BCM organisations in October 1977?
flashcard_questions.a: The apartheid government banned all major Black Consciousness organisations

flashcard_questions.q: How did BCM relate to the ANC?
flashcard_questions.a: BCM emphasised black self-organisation; the ANC had a multiracial philosophy — their relationship was sometimes tense

flashcard_questions.q: What was Mamphela Ramphele's contribution to BCM?
flashcard_questions.a: She helped organise community health clinics and welfare initiatives in townships

glossary_terms.definition: A movement founded by Steve Biko arguing that black South Africans must reject psychological oppression and assert pride in their own identity before political liberation is possible.
Student activist who founded SASO in 1969 and became the defining voice of the Black Consciousness Movement; died in police custody on 12 September 1977.
South African Students' Organisation — the Black Consciousness student body founded by Steve Biko in 1969 at black universities.
A broader political umbrella body founded in 1972 to spread Black Consciousness ideas beyond university campuses.
Activist and doctor who worked alongside Biko in the Black Consciousness Movement and later became a prominent figure in South African public life.
A sustained wave of industrial action by approximately 100,000 black workers in Durban from January to March 1973, which shook the apartheid government's confidence in controlling black labour.
